summary.en: Break work into static methods and trace value passing, overloads and recursion.
summary.bn: static মেথডে কাজ ভাগ করো এবং প্যারামিটারের কপি, ওভারলোড আর রিকার্শন বোঝো।

notes: Static methods, overloading and recursion here use long-established Java syntax.

sections.title: Give a repeated calculation a name
Read a declaration as a promise
A copy of a reference is still a copy
Read each call from inputs to returned control
Distinguish a result from a side effect
Name work and follow copied values

examples.title: A reusable credit calculation
examples.explanationHtml: The two int arguments are copied into the parameters. return sends 12 back to the caller.

examples.title: Primitive arguments are copied
examples.explanationHtml: raise changes its local value to 65. The caller still holds 60.

examples.title: Array mutation and reassignment
examples.explanationHtml: The copied reference first reaches the original array and changes 60 to 70. Reassigning the parameter cannot replace the caller reference.

examples.title: Two overloads
examples.explanationHtml: The int argument selects the int overload and prints 6. The double argument selects the double overload and prints 7.0.

examples.title: Recursive factorial
examples.explanationHtml: Each call reduces n until 1. Returning through the calls multiplies 2, 3, 4 and 5 to produce 120.

practice.title: Add a lab bonus
practice.statementHtml: Input: a mark from 0 to 95. A static addBonus method returns mark plus 5. Print the returned value.
hints: Use return to give a changed primitive back.

practice.title: The larger attendance
practice.statementHtml: Input: two counts from 0 to 30. Print the greater using a static maximum method.
hints: Both paths must return an int.

practice.title: Revise the first mark
practice.statementHtml: Input: n from 1 to 20, then n marks from 0 to 100. A static method changes the first mark to 100. Print that element after the call.
hints: Change the element reached through the reference, not the parameter itself.

practice.title: Recursive digit sum
practice.statementHtml: Input: a nonnegative integer up to 1000000000. Print the sum of its decimal digits using recursion.
hints: Dividing by ten removes one digit.

practice.title: Factorial with a limit
practice.statementHtml: Input: n from 0 to 20. Print n factorial using a recursive method returning long.
hints: A return type of long keeps 20 factorial within range.

quiz.prompt: Does changing a primitive parameter change the caller variable?
quiz.explanation: The method assigns its own parameter copy, leaving the caller x equal to 4.

quiz.prompt: Which array survives a parameter reassignment after mutation?
quiz.explanation: The mutation reaches the original array. Reassignment only changes the local parameter.

quiz.prompt: What result returns from sum(3) as the calls unwind?

quiz.explanation: Different parameter types distinguish overloads. Return type alone does not.

quiz.prompt: What does void mean in a method declaration?
quiz.explanation: A void method can perform actions and return control without a result value.

quiz.prompt: Why can a static helper be called from static main without an object?
options: main creates every object in advance
quiz.explanation: A static method belongs to the class rather than a particular instance.

quiz.prompt: What must a factorial recursion do before calling itself?
options: Handle a base case and reduce the argument
quiz.explanation: Without progress towards a base case, recursion keeps growing the call stack.

quiz.prompt: What is actually copied when an array is passed to a method?
options: Nothing; Java passes variables by reference
quiz.explanation: Java always passes values. A reference value identifies the same array after copying.

quiz.prompt: Which call selects scale(double) rather than scale(int)?
quiz.explanation: 2.5 is a double literal. An int argument selects the matching int overload.

quiz.prompt: What is a likely result of unbounded recursive calls?
quiz.explanation: Each call needs stack space; Java does not guarantee tail-call elimination.

quiz.prompt: Why can a factorial method still be wrong even with a correct stopping case?
options: Every recursive method must return void
A base case prevents all arithmetic errors
The numeric result may exceed its return type range
Java always converts long to unlimited precision
quiz.explanation: Termination and numeric range are separate obligations; long factorial is bounded.

quiz.prompt: How can a method offer a replacement array to its caller?
options: Return the new array and let the caller assign it
quiz.explanation: A returned reference lets the caller deliberately replace its variable.

keyPoints.en: A static method can be called through its class.
keyPoints.bn: static মেথড ক্লাসের নাম দিয়ে ডাকা যায়।

keyPoints.en: Java passes a copy of each argument value.
keyPoints.bn: জাভা প্রতিটি আর্গুমেন্টের মানের কপি পাঠায়।

keyPoints.en: A copied reference can still reach the same object.
keyPoints.bn: রেফারেন্সের কপি দিয়েও একই অবজেক্টে পৌঁছানো যায়।

keyPoints.en: Overloads differ in parameter lists, not only return types.
keyPoints.bn: ওভারলোডের প্যারামিটারের তালিকা আলাদা হয়, শুধু রিটার্ন টাইপ নয়।

keyPoints.en: Recursion needs a base case and progress towards it.
keyPoints.bn: রিকার্শনে থামার শর্ত আর সেই শর্তের দিকে এগোনো লাগে।

examQuestions.question: Prove with a trace that passing an array is still pass by value.
examQuestions.answerHtml: Draw a caller reference and a copied parameter reference pointing to one array. Element mutation is visible through both. Reassign the parameter to a new array; only its arrow moves. The caller arrow stays on the original array.

examQuestions.question: Why cannot return type alone distinguish overloaded methods?
examQuestions.answerHtml: Calls choose among parameter lists. A call used as a statement would not identify which return type to request. Java therefore rejects methods differing only in return type.

examQuestions.question: Trace factorial(4), including its stopping case.
examQuestions.answerHtml: factorial(4) requests 4 times factorial(3), then 3 times factorial(2), then 2 times factorial(1). The base case returns 1. Results return as 2, 6 and 24.
